summary:
Iğdır province stands under the national framework applicable across Turkey. No source in the current inventory reports conditions specific to Iğdır, so the findings below describe the regime a trans visitor would encounter anywhere in the country.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service. Conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' leaking publicly.

Since October 2018 governors have extended bans to LGBTI-focused events generally. Istanbul pride was banned repeatedly; police dispersed the 2015 and 2016 parades with water cannon and tear gas, and on 14 June 2019 the Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya prides were all banned.

In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities.

Amnesty International records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalize expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

A February 2026 press report stated that the government was considering a law criminalizing publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex' with a sentence of one to three years in prison; the measure was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill, the 12th judicial package.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern of event bans and prosecutions is national rather than local to Iğdır: governors across Turkey have issued LGBTI-focused event bans since October 2018, and the June 2025 Istanbul march bans and the December 2025 İzmir association dissolution illustrate how the regime operates in major western cities. Iğdır, a small eastern province on the Armenian and Iranian borders, has no documented equivalent case in the inventory, but the legal instruments enabling such action are national.

The draft legislative packages of 2025 and the February 2026 proposal on 'behavior contrary to biological sex' signal sustained executive hostility toward LGBTI expression, even where measures have not been enacted. Visitors should treat non-enactment as provisional rather than settled.
localsOnly:
Residents of Iğdır live under the same national rules on legal gender recognition (available since 1988), military service classification (openly LGBTQ people barred, conscripts declaring homosexuality assessed as a 'psychosexual illness' with photographic proof required and risk of a leaked 'unfit report'), and the absence of any comprehensive non-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised. Local LGBTI-focused events fall within the governor-level ban authority exercised since October 2018, and any association activity risks the kind of dissolution proceedings that an İzmir court ordered against the Young LGBTI+ Association in December 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the three 2025 draft law packages or the February 2026 proposal on 'behavior contrary to biological sex' has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources; the packages were not submitted to parliament as of the Amnesty report, and the February 2026 measure was excluded from the 12th judicial package.

No source in the inventory documents Iğdır-specific enforcement, incidents, or local official practice toward LGBTI or trans residents, so the province-level picture rests entirely on the national framework.
